newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Southwest monsoon still weak over Sri Lanka.
newsitem.headline: Southwest monsoon still weak over Sri Lanka.

text.p: The southwest monsoon which broke over Sri Lanka on Wednesday is still weak, the deputy director of the Meteorology Department, P.M. Jayatilaka Banda, told Reuters on Friday.
"The southwest monsoon is now established over the island but it is still weak," he said. "A depression has to form for the monsoon to strengthen but there is none in the island's vicinity."
There would be occasional showers in the southwestern part of the Indian Ocean island and evening thunderstorms in the Uva and Eastern provinces, he said.
Hydrocatchment areas, where the main power plants are located, were not getting much rain, he said.

Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) state power utility officials were not immediately available for comment. But the board has said it is confident of avoiding power cuts because it had commissioned new thermal power plants and plans to commission more later this year.
The CEB has said it plans to cut dependence on hydropower, which currently makes up 85 percent of grid power, to 57 percent after a crippling drought last year forced it to impose lengthy power cuts.
The CEB is building more thermal power plants and buying electricity from private plants.
Water levels in hydroreservoirs dropped to dangerously low levels again earlier this year with the failure of the northeast monsoon but improved after the delayed onset of intermonsoon showers.

Tropical Sri Lanka has two rainy seasons. The southwest monsoon, the most important for fuelling hydroelectricty plants and which usually starts by end-May, was delayed by about a week, the Meteorology Department said.
Sri Lanka has an installed capacity of 1,115 megawatts of hydropower and 250 megawatts of thermal power.
